sweep_summary: Jita (jita1239) is not in the catalog. The two title-hit items are Philippson's 1991 Paris 5 thesis on tone and accent in East African Bantu (comparative; Glottolog codes Jita among ~30 languages; theses.fr record saved, 'accessible: non', abstract only: a continuum from pure tone to demarcative penultimate stress, with penultimate accent as the diachronic driver) and Downing's 1995 LINCOM chapter on the metrical domain of register raising in Jita (OT tone/metrical-domain analysis; no online copy anywhere checked: ROA, archive.org, Open Library, ORCID, gup.ub.gu.se, HathiTrust/Google Books blocked). Both remain unread; both are medium-priority print acquisitions (Downing 1995 the more Jita-specific; Philippson 1991 more likely to give a one-line prosodic-type classification of Jita). All readable first-hand Jita sources already held by the project from our earlier reading (Downing 1988, 2014; Kagaya 2003 abstract, 2005; SIL 2016 orthography statement and grammar basics) are tone descriptions silent on word stress; Downing 2004 leaves Jita out of her Bantu stress-accent table and only reports Kenstowicz 1993's stress-analogy for Jita H tone. No first-hand stress statement found; the best new statement = none. Google, Bing, Brave, DuckDuckGo could not be reached by automated download) limited discovery to API/repository downloads; files and records with updated.

new_statements.quote: [Annexe: Résumé des systèmes prosodiques, PDF p.501; rubric key PDF p.497: '3. système tonal ou accentuel ... 10. statut de la syllabe pénultième'] groupe VI / Jita : 1. : oui / 3. : langue accentuelle à mélodie H / 4. : 3 / ... / 8. : H s'associe à chaque syllabe marquée / ... / 10. : accent démarcatif (culmination d'intensité et allongement plus sensible). [Ch.6 §3.5.2, PDF pp.483-484] quelque chose de très semblable est perceptible en jita et en ruri (groupe VI), où une longueur en syllabe pénultième de mot ressort beaucoup plus qu'une longueur située dans une syllabe précédente (...); une syllabe pénultième brève est également mise en valeur par un léger allongement, mais ici, bien plus nettement devant pause absolue.
new_statements.translation: Group VI / Jita: 1 [surface length contrast]: yes; 3: accentual language with an H melody; 4: 3 [prosodic patterns for disyllabic noun stems]; 8: an H associates to every marked syllable; 10 [status of the penultimate syllable]: demarcative accent (culmination of intensity and more noticeable lengthening). [Ch.6 §3.5.2] something very similar is perceptible in Jita and Ruri (group VI), where length in the word-penultimate syllable stands out much more than length in an earlier syllable (...); a short penultimate syllable is also brought out by a slight lengthening, but here much more clearly before absolute pause.

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record. The catalog has no Jita record and no stress statement is held by the project (all eight read sources are tagged 'silent on stress'); this is the first statement: demarcative penultimate accent (intensity + lengthening) coexisting with a lexical H-accent/tone system. It is consistent with the general East-Bantu penultimate-prominence pattern the thesis argues for and does not conflict with the tonal analyses held by the project (Downing 1990/1996/2014, Kagaya 2003/2004), which describe the tone system.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Philippson classes Jita (group VI, Suguti; his own field data) as an 'accentual language with an H melody': lexically, morphemes carry at most a mark (three prosodic patterns for disyllabic noun stems, BB/BH/HB) and an H tone associates to each marked syllable, with post-lexical tone shift one syllable to the right except from the penult/final before pause (ch.4 §4.2, p.131: 'le jita (analysable, lui aussi, comme langue à accent) n'applique pas la règle de déplacement aux deux dernières syllabes devant pause'; ch.6 p.484: 'jita et ruri : un H associé à la pénultième échappe au déplacement tonal (en jita, devant pause absolue)'). Independently of the tonal marks, the word-penultimate syllable bears a demarcative accent realised as an intensity peak and extra lengthening (long penults stand out more than long vowels elsewhere; short penults are slightly lengthened, most clearly before absolute pause). So: predictable, non-contrastive penultimate prominence (stress-like, demarcative) in a reduced tone / H-accent system.
new_statements.exceptions: No lexical exceptions to the penultimate demarcative accent are given. Tonal detail: an H on the penult (or final) does not shift rightward before absolute pause (in Ruri it never shifts); a final H retracts onto the second mora of a long all-Low penult (p.485: 'rwanda/rundi; jita; nilyamba : un H final est rétracté sur la deuxième more d'une syllabe pénultième longue et entièrement B'); a marked syllable before pause is realised with a falling tone (p.132). The author notes his Jita data do not allow the number of post-lexical strata to be fixed precisely (p.339).
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's Jita is E25 (JE25) of his group VI 'Suguti' (with Ruri, Kwaya, Regi), spoken on the south-east shore of Lake Victoria, Tanzania; data are his own field notes from the 1970s Dar es Salaam survey (word lists and sentences; he flags them as limited for post-lexical strata). Ruri is summarised as 'identique au jita' except that a penult/final H never shifts.

tone_statements.citation: Downing, Laura J. (1989). Tone in Jita questions. Studies in the linguistic sciences 19. pp. 91-113.
tone_statements.quote: [p.91] In Jita, an E. Bantu language spoken in Tanzania, yes-no questions are realized at a higher pitch than declaratives. [p.94] In (1a), the declarative, we find only high and low tones (high-toned syllables are marked with an acute accent; low-toned syllables are unmarked). But in (1b), the corresponding yes/no question, we find three tone levels: a raised high tone, [...]; a raised low tone, [...]; and a low tone, again unmarked. [p.111] The intonational rules which apply to yes/no questions are, first, grid-building rules which assign prominence to either the rightmost high tone or, if there are no high tones, the penult syllable of the utterance.

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale.

sources.note: Mrangi (northern) dialect. Outline of Grammar §1 Phonemes (p. 10): short/long vowels; 'A vowel before a prenasalized consonant /NC/ tends to be long. Especially, it is definitely long when the vowel before a prenasalized consonant is placed on the penultimate syllable of a word.' §4 Tone (pp. 12-13): two level tones L and H, F/R on long syllables, four noun tone types. sources.note: Secondary survey by the primary describer. p. 102: Jita (Downing 1996) cited among languages 'described as accentual or non-tonal by earlier scholars which are currently accepted as having tone'. Jita is absent from Table (15) 'Summary table of stress-accent in Bantu languages' (pp. 121-122). pp. 125-128 treat Jita H-tone culminativity, Meeussen's Rule and tone shift as pitch accent-like properties; p. 128: 'Kenstowicz (1993) argues that delinking is best explained if High tone in Jita is analogous to stress accent.'
